views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Proceed with a targeted Section 301 tariff package sized to the documented IP/tech-transfer harm (the $30–60 billion range already under White House consideration), aimed at Chinese industrial-policy and technology goods rather than a broad consumer sweep. Keep 232 country exemptions moving for security partners so the China IP case is not buried under an ally fight, and leave a negotiation channel open after tariffs are announced—do not offer purchase commitments or a rollback before Beijing tables structural IP remedies. Hold investment-restriction and visa measures until Treasury finishes a legally defensible, sector-narrowed design.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is scored as a moderate US opportunity, not a high or existential hit. The dispute is still US-initiated: the August 2017 Section 301 probe, the November 2017 Beijing visit that produced MOUs but “no substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer,” January Section 201 solar/washer tariffs, and the March 8 Section 232 steel/aluminum proclamations (China is a small direct steel supplier). US macros as of mid-March 2018 show no trade-war bite—Michigan sentiment 101.4, industrial production rising to 102.2, CPI contained, VIX back to 17.86 after the February spike, and CNY stronger at 6.32 rather than a depreciation shock. The goods deficit remains large (BOPGTB about −$70 billion; 2017 China goods gap $375.2 billion), which is the political and commercial backdrop, not a recession signal. The underlying IP problem is real and is why action is justified: USTR’s four 301 theories (JV/equity-forced transfer, discriminatory licensing, state-directed US tech acquisitions, cyber theft), Commission-on-IP-Theft estimates putting China at roughly $150–240 billion of annual US IP loss, and Navarro’s $600 billion upper bound. Beijing declined 301 consultations and offered no structural fix. That combination is leverage, not US vulnerability—hence a negative threat score, milder than −0.5 because China is not overextended, 232 is poorly aimed at China, and retaliation risk is already explicit. Action is moderate tariff escalation, not hold/negotiate and not maximal: Lighthizer told Ways & Means on March 21 that China retaliation (especially agriculture) is “inevitable” and that inaction is how the deficit persists; CNBC/Hill/LAT (March 21) had the White House teeing up a Thursday 301 announcement, with Trump pushing toward ~$60 billion but law tying remedies to estimated harm. China has already named US soybeans a “prime target” (~$12–14 billion; ASA/Reuters March 9), opened a sorghum AD/CVD probe, and pledged to “defend its interests.” Farm-belt exposure and ally anger over global 232 (Covington March 15: EU/Japan less willing to join a coordinated China IP track) are why the package should stay targeted and paired with 232 exemptions—not a trillion-dollar list, entity-list blast, or student-visa cut that sources said the President was already deferring. Concede_purchases or rollback would surrender leverage after Beijing already walked away from structural talks.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation complete and White House announcement imminent (Mar 21); Beijing visit produced no structural IP concessions
US real economy still strong (sentiment 101.4, rising IP, contained CPI); dispute not yet biting macros
Documented China IP/tech-transfer and cyber-theft costs vs record $375B goods deficit — genuine leverage issue, not US distress
China already signaling soybean/ag retaliation; 232 is global and poorly targeted at China (~2% of US steel imports)
Ally cohesion at risk if 232 and 301 stack; investment/visa tools not legally ready

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.
Trump signs Section 232 proclamations imposing the steel (25%) and aluminum (10%) tariffs.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment 101.4 as of 2018-03-01 — expansion-level confidence, no trade-war hit yet.
US industrial production 102.2067 (2018-03), still rising over the 180-day window.
US goods trade deficit still large at -$69,809 million (2018-03), after a run near -$73 to -$75 billion.
CNY/USD 6.32 on 2018-03-21, yuan stronger vs ~6.62 in late September — no FX-stress signal.
White House to announce 301 actions Thursday; Trump pushed tariffs on ~$60B; Lighthizer said China ag retaliation is inevitable and inaction yields the deficit.
ASA: Chinese officials said US soybeans are a prime target for retaliation against steel/aluminum tariffs.
Administration weighing 301 tariffs on 100+ Chinese products and investment restrictions; 301 has broader internal buy-in than 232.
March 15: 301 action imminent; concern that 232 steel/aluminum tariffs make EU and Japan less willing to coordinate on China IP.
US-China goods deficit hit a record $375.2 billion in 2017.
